verdict.rationale: GitBook documents its own visual web editor ('Block-based visual editor', 'AI-native visual editor ... with ... Git workflows built in') and first-party GitHub/GitLab Sync. Its docs say teams can 'Write in the editor ... or sync from Git', and a community user praises the web-based editor. The evidence never explicitly states that edits made in the visual editor are committed back to the Git repository, so the shared single-source-of-truth part is only implied. missing for 10: explicit documentation that editor changes write back bidirectionally to the synced Git repo, details on how non-technical edits are reviewed and merged into the same source (e.g., change requests mapping to commits or PRs), and independent hands-on corroboration of the editor-to-Git round trip.

support.subject: As a technical writer, non-technical teammates can edit docs in a visual web editor without touching git, and their changes flow into the same source of truth

citations.quote: GitBook’s AI-native visual editor makes it easy to write, review, and publish technical content — with Markdown, real-time collaboration, version control, and Git workflows built in
Write in the editor, drive it from your agent, or sync from Git.
The web-based book editor is phenomenal
